segments.script: What flows through 100,000 kilometres of vessels, carries oxygen to every cell, and fights every infection? Blood — your fluid connective tissue.
segments.video_prompt: Cinematic slow-motion animation inside a blood vessel. RBCs (red biconcave discs) flow in a stream. A large WBC (round, nucleated) tumbles slowly. Platelets (tiny irregular fragments) glitter. Golden bioluminescent lighting, deep-red vessel walls. Camera tracks alongside the cells.

segments.script: Blood has two components. Plasma (55%): water, albumin, globulins, fibrinogen, plus solutes. Formed elements (45%): RBCs are biconcave, anucleate, haemoglobin-containing, 4.5 to 5.5 million per mm³, lifespan 120 days, made in red bone marrow, destroyed in the spleen. WBCs are nucleated and amoeboid, 4,000 to 11,000 per mm³. Granulocytes: neutrophils (60–70%, phagocytise bacteria), basophils (histamine and heparin), eosinophils (anti-parasitic). Agranulocytes: lymphocytes B and T (antibody and cell-mediated immunity), monocytes (become macrophages). Platelets: anucleate cell fragments, 2.5 lakh per mm³, essential for blood clotting. Lymph: filtered plasma that leaks into interstitial space, collected by lymphatic capillaries, processed in lymph nodes, returned to blood via the thoracic duct.
segments.video_prompt: Infographic animation sequence: A test tube fills with blood — plasma (golden) separates above the red cell layer. Then zoom into formed elements — RBCs (biconcave red discs), WBCs explode into a branching tree (granulocytes left: neutrophil, basophil, eosinophil; agranulocytes right: lymphocyte B and T, monocyte), platelets (tiny fragments). Each branch has a function icon (phagocyte, shield, scissors). Then a lymph circulation diagram: capillary wall leakage → interstitial fluid → lymph capillary → lymph node (filtering icon) → thoracic duct → subclavian vein. Dark lab background, neon labels.
